blocks.text: A 34-year-old man with a long history of migraine is sent home from an emergency department with 'another migraine'. Two days later he returns after a collapse; a scan shows a subarachnoid haemorrhage. The first doctor was not careless: they met a familiar label and stopped looking for a different story.

blocks.markdown: Most diagnostic errors are not failures of knowledge. They are failures of **reasoning under pressure**: we reach conclusions quickly using mental shortcuts (heuristics), which are usually efficient and occasionally disastrous. This unit teaches you to recognise the commonest shortcuts that go wrong (cognitive biases), to deliberately interrupt your own reasoning with a **diagnostic time-out**, and to protect patients you send home using **safety-netting**.

blocks.title: Cognitive bias and diagnostic error
blocks.text: A **cognitive bias** is a systematic pattern of deviation in judgement caused by a mental shortcut. A **diagnostic error** is a diagnosis that is missed, wrong or unacceptably delayed. Bias is one cause of diagnostic error; system factors (poor handover, missing results, interruptions) are others.

blocks.markdown:
### Two modes of thinking

Dual-process theory describes **System 1** (fast, intuitive, pattern-recognition) and **System 2** (slow, analytical, effortful). Experienced clinicians rely heavily on System 1, which is right most of the time. Errors cluster when we are tired, rushed, interrupted or emotionally invested, because System 2 is not called in to check System 1.

blocks.caption: Common cognitive biases in clinical reasoning
rows: Anchoring
Locking onto an early impression and failing to adjust as new information arrives
Ask what finding does not fit; revisit the diagnosis when the picture changes
Premature closure
Accepting a diagnosis before it has been verified and stopping the search
Pause before finalising; ask what else could cause this
Confirmation bias
Seeking or over-weighting evidence that supports the favoured diagnosis and discounting the rest
Actively look for disconfirming evidence
Availability bias
Over-estimating the likelihood of a diagnosis because a recent or dramatic case comes readily to mind
Think about base rates and the actual features of this patient
Diagnostic momentum
A label passed from one clinician or document to the next becomes accepted as fact
Treat inherited labels as hypotheses and re-take key parts of the history
Framing effect
Being swayed by how a case is presented (for example 'a frequent attender')
Re-describe the problem in neutral terms
Search satisficing
Stopping the search once one abnormality is found, missing a second
Ask whether the finding explains everything

blocks.title: Naming the bias in a ward case
blocks.prompt: A 71-year-old woman on a surgical ward is labelled 'post-operative confusion' in the notes by the night team. The morning doctor reads this, notes she is drowsy and writes 'delirium, continue to observe'. Her capillary glucose is not checked. She is on insulin. Which biases are operating, and what would break the chain?

steps.text: Identify the origin of the label: it was assigned by another clinician and copied forward without re-examination. This is diagnostic momentum.
Identify the doctor's own reasoning: a plausible and common explanation (post-operative delirium) was accepted without testing alternatives. This is premature closure.
Check for anchoring: the 'confusion' label drew attention away from a treatable, quickly testable cause (hypoglycaemia in an insulin-treated patient).

Choose the safeguard: treat the inherited label as a hypothesis, re-take the story, and check simple reversible causes first. A capillary glucose takes seconds and is part of assessing any altered consciousness.

blocks.answer: Diagnostic momentum, premature closure and anchoring. The chain is broken by re-assessing independently and checking reversible causes such as glucose.

blocks.title: Feeling certain is not evidence
blocks.text: Confidence and accuracy are only loosely related. The commonest moment for a bias to bite is when a case feels obvious and you are busy. A sense of 'this is straightforward' is a cue to check, not to relax.

blocks.markdown:
### The diagnostic time-out

A **diagnostic time-out** is a deliberate pause, borrowed from the surgical safety checklist, in which you step out of fast thinking and test your leading diagnosis. It takes under a minute. Use it when the patient is not improving as expected, when a result does not fit, before discharge, and when you are about to commit to a label that someone else gave you.

items: State the working diagnosis and the evidence that supports it.
Ask: what findings do NOT fit?
Ask: what is the worst thing this could be, and what else could cause this picture? Name at least two alternatives, including one dangerous 'cannot miss' diagnosis.
Ask: has anything changed since the diagnosis was made (new symptoms, new results, failure to respond to treatment)?
Decide what single action would best separate the leading diagnosis from the main alternative, and who you will ask for a second opinion if still unsure.

blocks.title: A diagnostic time-out in action
blocks.prompt: A 47-year-old man is diagnosed with 'muscular back pain' after lifting a box. Four days later he returns: the pain is no better, he has noticed difficulty passing urine, and numbness around the buttocks. The doctor's first instinct is to repeat the analgesia. Run a time-out.

steps.text: Working diagnosis: mechanical back pain. Supporting evidence: onset after lifting, no previous history.
What does not fit? Failure to improve, new urinary symptoms and perineal numbness. These are red flags and are not explained by simple muscle strain.

Alternatives and the cannot-miss diagnosis: cauda equina compression (for example from a disc prolapse) is the dangerous alternative because delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.
What has changed? New neurological symptoms have appeared since the original diagnosis, so the original label must be reopened.
Action: do not repeat analgesia. Examine neurologically including perianal sensation and arrange urgent senior review and emergency imaging according to local pathway.

blocks.answer: The time-out reveals that the new red-flag features contradict the working diagnosis. Cauda equina syndrome must be excluded urgently by senior review and imaging.

blocks.markdown:
### Safety-netting when patients go home

No diagnosis is certain at the point of discharge: many illnesses declare themselves only with time. **Safety-netting** is advice given to patients (and recorded) that tells them what to watch for, how quickly to act, and whom to contact if things change. It converts uncertainty into a plan, and it is a recognised safeguard against diagnostic error because the patient becomes part of the detection system.

blocks.caption: Elements of effective safety-netting
rows: What to look out for
Specific symptoms, not 'if you get worse'
Patients cannot act on vague advice
Time frame
'If not improving within 48 hours' or 'immediately if...'
Gives an expected course and a trigger
Who and how to contact
Named service, telephone number, when to call emergency services
Removes barriers to re-attendance
Understanding check
Ask the patient or carer to repeat the plan in their own words
Confirms the message was received
Documentation
Record the advice and who it was given to in the notes
Supports continuity and shows what was communicated
Provided in suitable form
Written leaflet, translated or interpreted where needed
Anxious or unwell patients forget verbal advice

blocks.title: Link the three safeguards
blocks.text: Name the biases to notice them, run a time-out to interrupt them, and use safety-netting to catch what you could not resolve. Each covers a different point in the patient's journey: before the decision, at the decision, and after the decision.

points: Diagnostic errors usually arise from reasoning shortcuts rather than lack of knowledge; common biases include anchoring, premature closure, confirmation bias, availability bias, diagnostic momentum and framing.
A diagnostic time-out deliberately tests the leading diagnosis: what does not fit, what is the cannot-miss alternative, and what has changed.
Safety-netting gives specific, time-framed advice on what to watch for and whom to contact, checks understanding, and is documented.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with epigastric discomfort and labelled 'gastritis' in the clerking. Three doctors in turn write 'gastritis, continue PPI' without re-taking the history. Which bias best describes the repeated acceptance of the original label?

options.text: Diagnostic momentum
Availability bias
Framing effect
Search satisficing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a label gains weight as it passes from clinician to clinician without independent checking.
distractorRationale.b: Availability bias is driven by recent or memorable cases coming to mind, which is not described here.
distractorRationale.c: Framing effect concerns how the case is presented, not repeated copying of a label.
distractorRationale.d: Search satisficing is stopping after finding one abnormality, not inheriting a label.

questions.explanation: Diagnostic momentum occurs when a provisional diagnosis is passed along and hardens into apparent fact because no one re-tests it. The remedy is to treat inherited labels as hypotheses and re-take the key history.

questions.stem: A doctor believes a patient's breathlessness is due to heart failure. Reviewing the case, she mentally records the raised JVP and ignores the clear, unilateral reduced breath sounds and a pleural-type pain. This pattern is best described as:

options.text: Confirmation bias
Availability bias
Diagnostic momentum
Framing effect

distractorRationale.a: Correct: she favours findings that support her hypothesis and discounts those that do not.
distractorRationale.b: Availability bias would require a memorable recent case driving the estimate; none is described.
distractorRationale.d: No particular presentation or label from a referrer is described.

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and weigh evidence that supports the favoured diagnosis while discounting contrary findings. The corrective step is to ask explicitly which findings do not fit.

questions.stem: A junior doctor has just attended a patient with a pulmonary embolism missed by a colleague. For the next week she requests CT pulmonary angiography for almost every breathless patient, including those with clear alternative causes. Which bias is most likely at work?

options.text: Anchoring on the first piece of information in each case
Availability bias
Premature closure
Diagnostic momentum

distractorRationale.a: Anchoring concerns the first impression within a case, not the influence of a recent case.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a vivid recent case makes that diagnosis seem more probable than the base rate warrants.
distractorRationale.c: Premature closure is stopping the search too early, not over-investigating.
distractorRationale.d: No label is being handed on between clinicians.

questions.explanation: Availability bias distorts probability estimates according to how easily examples come to mind. It can cause over-diagnosis as well as missed diagnosis, so the countermeasure is to reason from the patient's actual features and base rates.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best description of a diagnostic time-out?

options.text: A planned pause to test the leading diagnosis, ask what does not fit and consider dangerous alternatives
A period during which the clinician stops seeing patients after a diagnostic error
A request for every possible investigation so that no diagnosis can be missed
A formal meeting held weeks later to review an incident

questions.correctOptionText: A planned pause to test the leading diagnosis, ask what does not fit and consider dangerous alternatives

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is a brief deliberate pause that engages analytical thinking.
distractorRationale.b: A time-out is a reasoning tool, not a suspension from work.
distractorRationale.c: Indiscriminate testing is not a time-out and can cause harm.
distractorRationale.d: A retrospective review is a different process, whereas a time-out happens in real time.

questions.explanation: The diagnostic time-out is a real-time check built on the same principle as the surgical safety pause. It engages System 2 thinking at the moment when the diagnosis is still open to change.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had three days of sore throat treated as tonsillitis. She now has severe throat pain with muffled voice, trismus and drooling to one side, and her temperature is higher despite antibiotics. During a time-out, which action best uses the principles taught in this unit?

options.text: Increase the dose of the same antibiotic because the working diagnosis is common and probably correct
Treat the failure to improve and the new features as findings that do not fit, consider a deep neck space infection such as peritonsillar abscess, and seek urgent senior or ENT assessment
Reassure her and ask her to return in a week if the symptoms persist
Wait for the next set of blood tests before reconsidering the diagnosis

questions.correctOptionText: Treat the failure to improve and the new features as findings that do not fit, consider a deep neck space infection such as peritonsillar abscess, and seek urgent senior or ENT assessment

distractorRationale.a: This is anchoring: a common diagnosis is kept despite evidence of failure to respond.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it asks what does not fit, names a dangerous alternative and escalates.
distractorRationale.c: Reassurance and delay ignores new red-flag features.
distractorRationale.d: Waiting for results delays reconsideration when the examination already contradicts the label.

questions.explanation: A time-out asks what does not fit and what dangerous alternative exists; failure to improve with trismus and drooling points to a complication needing urgent specialist assessment. The common label (tonsillitis) should be treated as a hypothesis that has been challenged.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with a viral-type illness is discharged from the paediatric assessment unit. Which discharge advice is the best example of safety-netting?

options.text: 'He should be fine, but come back if you are worried.'

'If he develops a rash that does not fade under a glass, is drowsy or hard to wake, or is not drinking for 8 hours, call 999 or return to the emergency department straight away. If the fever lasts beyond 5 days, see your GP.' The parent repeats this back and it is documented.
'Give paracetamol and see how it goes.'
A leaflet is placed in the bag without discussion.

questions.correctOptionText: 'If he develops a rash that does not fade under a glass, is drowsy or hard to wake, or is not drinking for 8 hours, call 999 or return to the emergency department straight away. If the fever lasts beyond 5 days, see your GP.' The parent repeats this back and it is documented.

distractorRationale.a: Too vague: it gives no specific triggers or timescale.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: specific symptoms, time frames, who to contact, understanding checked and documented.
distractorRationale.c: This is treatment advice but offers no triggers for re-assessment.
distractorRationale.d: A leaflet without discussion does not check understanding.

questions.explanation: Good safety-netting is specific about symptoms and timing, says whom to contact and how urgently, checks the carer's understanding and is recorded. Vague statements such as 'come back if worried' do not tell the carer what actually matters.

questions.stem: True or false: safety-netting advice is only necessary when the doctor is uncertain about the diagnosis, because a confident diagnosis cannot be wrong.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Confidence does not guarantee accuracy, and many illnesses evolve after discharge. Safety-netting is a routine safeguard that protects patients when the diagnosis is wrong or the illness changes.

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by anchoring and premature closure, state how they differ, and describe how a diagnostic time-out reduces the risk of each.
markingGuide: Anchoring: fixing on an early impression or piece of information and failing to adjust when new evidence arrives
Premature closure: accepting a diagnosis before it is verified and stopping the search for alternatives
Distinction: anchoring concerns insufficient updating from an initial impression; premature closure concerns ending the diagnostic process too early
Time-out for anchoring: asks what has changed and what does not fit the working diagnosis
Time-out for premature closure: forces consideration of alternatives, including a dangerous cannot-miss diagnosis
Mentions that the time-out is brief, deliberate and engages analytical (System 2) thinking
questions.explanation: Both biases arise from fast intuitive reasoning going unchecked. The time-out introduces a structured pause that makes the clinician revisit evidence and alternatives before committing, which is why it interrupts both patterns.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a diagnosis of renal colic is about to be discharged from the emergency department. Describe the safety-netting advice you would give and explain why it is a safeguard against diagnostic error.
markingGuide: Specific red-flag symptoms to watch for: fever or rigors, vomiting, pain not controlled by the prescribed analgesia, inability to pass urine
States that these may suggest infection above an obstruction or other diagnosis and need urgent review
Gives a time frame and route for re-attendance, including whom to contact and when to use emergency services
Checks understanding by asking the patient to repeat the advice back and uses written information
Documents the advice and the person who received it in the notes
Explains that the diagnosis was provisional and the patient becomes part of the detection system for evolving illness or alternative diagnoses
questions.explanation: Renal colic can be mimicked by other conditions and can be complicated by infection in an obstructed system. Safety-netting makes sure that if the picture changes, the patient knows what to look for and how fast to act, which catches errors that the clinician could not resolve at discharge.

questions.stem: Describe the steps of a diagnostic time-out and say at which points in a patient's hospital stay you would deliberately use one.
markingGuide: State the working diagnosis and its supporting evidence
Ask which findings do not fit
Name alternative diagnoses, including a dangerous cannot-miss condition
Ask what has changed since the diagnosis was made, such as new symptoms or results
Decide an action that separates the leading diagnosis from the alternatives or seek a second opinion
Examples of when to use: patient not improving, result does not fit, before discharge, when inheriting a label from another team
questions.explanation: The time-out is short and structured so it can be used routinely. Its value lies in being triggered by specific cues such as failure to respond or a mismatch between findings and diagnosis.
